extracted.intended_audience: The People of the State of New York (voters/ratifiers considering the proposed U.S. Constitution)
extracted.subtask_description: An 18th‑century Federalist essay arguing why the proposed U.S. Senate's design (qualifications, mode of appointment, equal representation, size, term, and powers) is necessary to secure stability, guard against faction, and preserve national character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity in the time of elections for the federal House of Representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformity in the time of elections for the federal House of Representatives is a positive advantage resulting from the proposed disposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If each State may choose its own time of election there could be as many different periods as months in the year (times vary between March and November). This diversity prevents a total dissolution or renovation of the body at one time, lets an improper spirit infuse successive new members, and thus perpetuates the same mass. Uniform timing is also requisite for executing regular rotation in the Senate and for convening the legislature at a stated annual period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for senators
rubrics_metrics.description: Senators must be at least thirty years old and citizens for nine years (as opposed to representatives: 25 years old and 7 years' citizenship).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A more advanced age and longer citizenship period are justified because the senatorial trust requires greater information and stability of character and relates to foreign transactions—so senators should be weaned from prepossessions of foreign birth/education. Nine years is a prudent mediocrity between excluding adopted citizens altogether and admitting them too hastily, guarding against foreign influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment of senators by State legislatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Senators are appointed by State legislatures rather than directly by the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mode favors a select appointment and gives State governments an agency in forming the federal government, securing the authority of the states and forming a convenient link between state and federal systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of representation in the Senate
rubrics_metrics.description: Each State receives an equal vote in the Senate — an ingredient of compromise between large and small states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equality is a constitutional recognition of residuary sovereignty in the states and an instrument for preserving it. In a compound republic mixing national and federal characters, a mixture of proportional and equal representation is defensible. The equal vote also adds an impediment against improper legislation because no law can pass without a majority of the people and a majority of the States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of senators and duration of appointment (stability and purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate should be less numerous and its members hold longer terms (six years) to supply purposes a senate is intended to answer: stability, firmness, and permanence of attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A senate doubles security by dividing legislative power, corrects the impulse of sudden and violent passions in large assemblies, and should be distinguished by circumstances consistent with harmony and republican principles. Less numerous bodies are better able to avoid factional impulses and maintain firmness through longer tenure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate as a double security/check on government
rubrics_metrics.description: Having a second legislative body (the Senate) provides an additional check on the government, requiring concurrence of two distinct bodies to carry schemes of usurpation or perfidy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This precaution increases the improbability of sinister combinations; the dissimilarity in genius between the two bodies enhances the check. The Senate's existence is a salutary check in all cases to the first branch's potential misdeeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate should be less numerous and possess firmness
rubrics_metrics.description: A body intended to correct factious impulses must itself be free from those impulses — i.e., less numerous and holding authority by considerable duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large, frequently elected assemblies are prone to sudden passions and intemperate resolutions; the corrective body must be small and durable to resist such tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate supplies legislative knowledge and continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: A senate remedies the defect that ordinary representatives, chosen briefly and from private pursuits, lack the time and motive to study laws and national affairs, leading to legislative blunders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many repealing, explaining, and amending laws reflect deficient wisdom caused by transient assemblies. A stable senate promotes long-run knowledge, reduces errors, and supports more coherent legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate prevents harmful mutability in public councils
rubrics_metrics.description: Stability in national policy is essential; frequent succession of new members produces mutability that harms foreign respect, internal order, and economic enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mutable government forfeits foreign respect, causes incoherent and constantly changing laws, advantages the sagacious and moneyed few over the uninformed many, discourages long-term investment and improvement, and diminishes popular attachment and reverence for government. A senate helps avoid these outcomes by providing continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate cultivates a sense of national character and attention to foreign opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The national councils need a due sense of national character; only a select and stable body can possess sensibility to the opinion of other nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attention to foreign judgment is desirable both to appear as the offspring of wise policy and to use foreign opinion as a guide in doubtful cases. A numerous and changeable body cannot sufficiently grasp such considerations; a senate can.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate provides responsibility for long-term measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Short-term assemblies cannot be properly responsible for long chains of connected measures whose effects unfold over years; a more permanent body is needed that can be answerable for such long-term objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsibility must be limited to objects within power and to operations constituents can judge; assemblies with very short terms cannot rightly be held accountable for multi-year programs. The remedy is an additional legislative body with sufficient permanency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate as a defense against popular errors and temporary passions
rubrics_metrics.description: A temperate, respectable body can check misguided popular motions and suspend measures until reason and justice regain authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are moments when the people, misled by passion or misrepresentation, call for measures they later regret; a senate can protect the people from such self-inflicted harms by delaying or checking rash actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical precedent supports the necessity of a senate
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-lived republics (Sparta, Rome, Carthage) historically had senates; their examples indicate the need for an institution that blends stability with liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though not fit to imitate in all respects, these cases show that republics without such an institution have had fugitive and turbulent existences. Ancient representative practices also demonstrate that 'representation' was not wholly unknown; the American distinction is the exclusion of the people in their collective capacity from national administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counter-argument: safeguards against the Senate becoming an aristocratic tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: The fear that an indirectly-appointed six‑year Senate will become an aristocratic tyranny is misplaced because such a transformation would require a sequence of corruptions (the Senate must corrupt itself, State legislatures, the House, and the people).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience (e.g., Maryland's Senate, British examples, and ancient history) suggests the practical checks and popular branch will prevent enduring aristocratic usurpation. The House of Representatives, with the people, can always restore constitutional principles if necessary.
